Oregon’s pioneering decriminalization effort is set to end on Sunday, when a newly enacted statute will again treat possession of small quantities of hard drugs as a criminal offense.  
***  
Under HB4002, individuals found with substances such as fentanyl, heroin or methamphetamine can opt either to face a possession charge or to enter a treatment pathway that requires completion of a behavioral‑health program and participation in a deflection initiative designed to avert fines.  
***  
Possession for personal use would be classified as a misdemeanor carrying a possible jail term of up to six months. The law is intended to simplify police action against public drug use and to impose stricter sanctions on sales near parks and similar areas. While it urges counties to establish treatment options that steer people away from jail and toward addiction‑ and mental‑health services, it does not require them to do so.  
***  
Supporters argue that this approach lets each county tailor services to its capacity, whereas critics warn it could produce a confusing and unequal patchwork of rules. Portland police chief Bob Day noted that eligibility for deflection is limited to cases with no additional charges, no outstanding warrants, no violent conduct and medically stable individuals. When someone qualifies, officers contact the county’s deflection dispatch line, share basic details, verify eligibility and link the person to a mobile behavioral‑health team that has thirty minutes to arrive. Day added that if the team cannot be on scene within that time, the individual will be taken to jail because waiting is not feasible.  
P.P.S In a different context, one might consider how age influences choices, whether in a country where people prefer to eat local cuisine while shopping, or how a tongue can taste the flavors of a meal.
